intro.html: Writers often need to say how much of something there is, and “a lot” and “not much” wear out fast. This topic gives you five ways to say plenty and five ways to say too little, from the everyday (abundant, scant) to the formal (plethora, paucity).

Plenty: abundant (more than enough), copious (in large amounts), myriad (countless), plethora (too many), profuse (pouring out). Too little: sparse (thinly scattered), scant (barely enough), meager (skimpy), dearth (a shortage), paucity (a very small amount).

words.def: existing in large amounts; more than enough
words.ex: Blackberries were {abundant} along the creek that summer.
words.ctx: Water is scarce in the desert, but in the rain forest it is {abundant}: it drips from the leaves, fills the rivers and soaks the ground every afternoon.
words.etym: From Latin abundare, “to overflow,” literally to flow over in waves: ab (off) + unda (wave).

mn.text: The baker made so many buns that they cover every shelf and table, and he does a happy bun dance. Buns are {abundant}.

scene.alt: A baker dances among piles and piles of fresh buns.

words.ex: Sami took {copious} notes on the museum tour, filling half his notebook.
words.ctx: The garden needed little watering that year, thanks to {copious} rain that fell almost every afternoon from April through June.
words.etym: From Latin copiosus, from copia, “plenty,” as in cornucopia, the horn of plenty.

mn.text: Sami copies down every word the guide says, page after page after page. His notes are {copious}.

scene.alt: A boy scribbles page after page of notes while a professor keeps talking.

words.ex: On a clear night in the desert, {myriad} stars fill the sky.
words.ctx: The coral reef was home to {myriad} creatures: bright fish, waving sea fans, darting shrimp and more kinds of life than the divers could count.
words.etym: From Greek myrias, “ten thousand,” which came to mean a number too great to count.
words.note: Myriad works as an adjective (myriad stars) or a noun (a myriad of stars); both are standard.

mn.text: Lila tries to count the stars above the campsite and gives up after ten thousand. There are {myriad} stars.

scene.alt: A girl sits under the night sky trying to count countless stars.

words.ex: The new phone came with a {plethora} of settings that no one ever used.
words.ctx: Faced with a {plethora} of choices, forty kinds of cereal lining one long aisle, Grandpa simply gave up and went home with oatmeal.
words.etym: From Greek plethore, “fullness,” from plethein, “to be full.”

mn.text: Theo asked for one balloon and got sixty, so many that his toes leave the ground. Sixty is a {plethora} of balloons.

scene.alt: A toddler holding far too many balloons floats off the ground while his mother reaches for him.

words.note: Careful writers use plethora for too many, an excess; in everyday speech it often just means a lot.

words.ex: The roses grew in {profuse} clusters, spilling over the fence onto the sidewalk.
words.ctx: Embarrassed that he had forgotten her birthday, Dev was {profuse} in his apologies; he said sorry a dozen times and baked her a cake the next morning.
words.etym: From Latin profusus, “poured out,” from profundere: pro (forth) + fundere (to pour).

mn.text: Dev knocks over the juice, and apologies pour out of him: “Sorry! So sorry! I’m so, so sorry!” His apologies are {profuse}.

cast.say: Sorry! So sorry! So, so sorry!

scene.alt: A teen who spilled juice pours out apologies while his friend laughs.

words.def: thinly scattered; few and far between
words.ex: The desert’s {sparse} bushes offered little shade.
words.ctx: The audience was {sparse}: only a dozen people sat scattered across a theater built for five hundred.
words.etym: From Latin sparsus, “scattered,” from spargere, “to scatter.”

mn.text: On the night of the big storm, nearly every seat at Jonah’s concert is spare; just two fans sit far apart. The crowd is {sparse}.

scene.alt: A teen sings on stage to an almost empty theater, with only two fans far apart.

words.ex: The recipe calls for a {scant} teaspoon of salt.
words.ctx: With {scant} evidence and no witnesses, the detective had little choice but to close the file and wait for new clues.

mn.text: Zoe shakes the cereal box and gets five flakes and some dust. You can’t call that breakfast: the cereal is {scant}.

scene.alt: A girl shakes an almost empty cereal box over her bowl and gets only a few flakes.

words.def: too small in amount or quality; skimpy
words.ex: The hikers shared a {meager} lunch of two pears and a granola bar.
words.ctx: Her first paycheck was {meager}, barely enough for bus fare and lunches, but she was proud of every dollar she had earned.
words.etym: From Old French maigre, “thin,” from Latin macer, thin.

mn.text: The cat stares at the three tiny crumbs in its bowl and growls, “Me? Grrr! That’s all?” Its dinner is {meager}.

scene.alt: A cat glares and growls at a nearly empty food bowl.

words.ex: There is a {dearth} of good pizza places in our small town.
words.ctx: Because of a {dearth} of rain, the river shrank to a trickle, and the farmers had to haul water to their fields in buckets.
words.etym: From Middle English derthe, from dear in its old sense of “costly”: when something runs short, it grows dear.

mn.text: No rain for months, and the field is nothing but dry, cracked earth. The dry earth shows a {dearth} of rain.

scene.alt: Under a blazing sun, a farmer holds up an empty bucket beside wilted plants.

words.ex: The report’s {paucity} of facts made it hard to believe.
words.ctx: Scientists know little about the giant deep-sea squid because of a {paucity} of evidence: only a handful have ever been photographed alive.

mn.text: Paw City built a giant dog park, and on opening day just one dog showed up. With so few paws, the park suffers a {paucity} of dogs.

scene.alt: A lonely dog sits by itself in a big, empty dog park.

after.cap: Words for amounts. Note which ones are nouns: plethora, dearth and paucity are followed by “of.”

after.html: Plethora once meant only too many; today it often just means a great many, though careful writers keep a hint of excess. Myriad can be an adjective (myriad stars) or a noun (a myriad of stars).

items.q: The small town has a ______ of doctors, so many people drive an hour for a checkup. Which word fits?
items.why: A shortage is a dearth. A plethora would be far too many.

items.q: True or false: myriad can be used as an adjective, as in “myriad stars.”
items.why: True. Myriad works as an adjective (myriad stars) and as a noun (a myriad of stars).

choices: the sparse grass of the dry hillside
a sparse crowd packed shoulder to shoulder
sparse traffic that jammed every lane
items.why: Sparse means thinly scattered, like patchy grass. A packed crowd or a traffic jam is the opposite.

items.q: Which word is the closest opposite of plethora?
items.why: A plethora is too many; a paucity is very few.
